articles.title: Why dodgy doors are the latest casualty of the UK heatwaves
articles.summary: Sticking or unlockable doors are yet another problem caused by the hot summer, but winter can also bring difficulties. Thursday was another busy day for Alan Hickman, a Bournemouth-based locksmith who works in the area around the New Forest (“though I’m currently dodging the bit between Ringwood…
body: Speaking on his way to see a man who can’t close his patio doors – “probably because they’ve got some expansion issues” – he then has a callout to see an elderly woman who needs a lockbox installed for her carer, before visiting a customer in Westbourne “to sort another composite door that can’t lock”.

Such cases of sticking, unopenable or unlockable doors are much more common at the moment, says Hickman, due, like so much else, to the very hot weather across much of the UK over the past few months.

“We’re getting what feels like double the amount of calls a day because customers’ doors just aren’t able to open, or they can’t close them at the end of a hot day until they’ve cooled down again,” he says. Hickman has worked with LockRite, one of the UK’s largest networks of uniformed locksmiths, for 14 years but this summer has “definitely brought a significant increase” in heat-related callouts.

articles.title: We’ll never be royals: the California town where Prince Harry and Meghan lived says goodbye
articles.summary: As the couple plans their return to the UK, Montecito’s whirlwind stint on the global stage may be coming to an end. The bucolic coastal California town of Montecito was thrust into the limelight six years ago as the backdrop for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s second act following an acrimonious…
body: But as the couple plans their return to the United Kingdom, Montecito’s whirlwind stint on the global stage may be coming to an end.

To be clear, the well-to-do enclave near Santa Barbara is unlikely to lose its reputation as a hideout for celebrities – a respite from the paparazzi den that Los Angeles, about 90 miles (145km) south, can be. Oprah, Gwyneth Paltrow and Ellen DeGeneres, among other public figures, have all resided in the tony community.

Prince Harry and Meghan, though, were arguably top contenders for Montecito’s most attention-grabbing residents. After news emerged that the couple had bought a $14.7m estate in the area, news helicopters and photographers swarmed in, to the annoyance of some neighbors.

Reporters even clamored for intel on a local Facebook page, prompting a moderator to warn journalists in a 2020 post: “No one will sell out or talk to the press. We don’t care who you are or where you came from, if you are our neighbor and act like a neighbor we support you.”

articles.title: The Business of Katseye
articles.summary: As the world’s first multi-ethnic, English-language group modeled on the K-pop framework, Katseye has broken significant industry barriers. Their continued high-profile activities indicate their ability to adapt despite recent controversy. But can their influence be sustained?
body: Three years ago, six young women — Sophia, Lara, Manon, Daniela, Megan and Yoonchae — were catapulted into instant global fame when they appeared on the Netflix reality show, The Debut: Dream Academy, beating 100,000 other contestants to be part of the pop group Katseye.

The premise was unusual. Formed through a joint venture between the South Korean music powerhouse Hybe and American record label Geffen Records, Katseye pioneered a unique cross-market model that applied Korea’s notorious idol bootcamp infrastructure with Western mainstream pop production. Their unique heritage was an added draw — the six members come from diverse countries including the US, Switzerland, the Philippines, and South Korea.

Also crucial to the group’s image-building was the insider fashion knowledge procured from close collaborators including creative director Humberto Leon, co-founder of the once-cult shopping destination Opening Ceremony and former co-designer at Kenzo, alongside stylist Katie Qian, whose clients include Tyla, Conan Gray, Camila Cabello, and Tinashe.
In an age where fame feels more accessible than ever, only a select few manage to break through the noise. Here’s what sets them apart.

articles.title: ‘If I’m spending that kind of money, the shoe has to do everything’ – the backlash to the three figure trainer
articles.summary: From Nike’s infamous 110s to £250 and back again, sneakerheads are rediscovering why cheaper shoes can be worth just as much hype as much more expensive ones. • Don’t get Fashion Statement delivered to your inbox? Sign up here.
body: When Nike’s Air Max 95 trainers first landed in Britain back in the mid-1990s, they looked unlike anything else. Created by footwear designer Sergio Lozano, the shoe had wavy layers running down its sides, neon yellow accents, and visible ‘Air’ bubbles underfoot. But in the UK, one detail quickly became as famous as the shoe itself: its £110 price tag.

The Air Max 95 immediately picked up the nickname “110” because spending £110 on trainers seemed outrageous at the time. Owning a pair quickly became a status symbol among young men across Britain, while in celebrity circles they were worn by everyone from Jay-Z to Kylie Minogue.

Over 30 years later, £110 looks relatively modest next to the upper end of the market catering to trainer enthusiasts. In a pretty neat example of trainerflation, flagship running shoes from Nike, New Balance, and Adidas easily retail for between £200 and £250.
points: From Nike’s infamous 110s to £250 and back again, sneakerheads are rediscovering why cheaper shoes can be worth just as much hype as much more expensive ones.

articles.title: I’ll admit it: I’ve cycled through red lights. But Britain’s traffic laws are to blame, not me | Simon Jenkins
articles.summary: The essence of cycling is to keep moving, but London’s chaotic roads often make this difficult. My solution: fewer, not more rules. I plead guilty. I have loved and used the streets of London all my life, as a cyclist, driver and pedestrian.
body: When I try to drive at the authorised speed of 20mph on many through roads, I am hooted at and overtaken by vans, cars, coaches and buses. And when I sit dutifully on my bike at a traffic light, I am jostled by swarms of cyclists riding through on red, furious at being treated as if they were car drivers.
As for pedestrians, walking on many pavements is like taking a ride on the dodgems. Riders of ebikes and e-scooters ignore bans and expect everyone to move out of the way.

I normally approve of anarchy. There is too much regulation everywhere. The great Dutch traffic engineer Hans Monderman boldly advocated “shared space” in cities. He wanted kerbs, road markings and traffic signals minimised and replaced by “human discipline”. All road users should navigate urban space by watching out for each other all the time. Monderman is virtually unknown in Britain, but principles similar to his were trialled with success in London’s Exhibition Road and Seven Dials. His counterintuitive ideas have been applied with remarkable success across northern Europe, with accidents falling. In 2023, 45% of Copenhageners cycled to work or school.

articles.title: This Underrated California Wine Country Will Transport You Straight to Europe
articles.summary: Want the feel of an Italian or Spanish vineyard vacation, without actually traveling across the Atlantic? Head to Temecula Valley Wine Country.
body: I cheekily open one eye to peer around during shavasana as I lay on my yoga mat between the vines’ full summer foliage at Akash Winery. I’m in Southern California, but the cypress trees and stucco homes suggest an amalgamation of a Tuscan-Provencal hilltop town. I return to darkness for my final deep breaths, grateful for the movement, before another day of wine tasting—which would begin less than five minutes after rolling up my mat and strolling to the tasting room for a breakfast sip of sparkling Sauvignon Blanc.

“Most areas have a signature varietal, but I don’t think we need to pigeonhole ourselves into a certain one,” says Justin Knight, winemaker at Danza Del Sol Winery, as we sip through a delicate yet fruity Albariño, native to Spain’s northwestern Rías Baixas region before switching gears to southern France for a subtly floral Viognier with a delightfully mineral finish.

articles.title: This Jewelry-Designer Bride Created All Her Own Looks for Her Tuscan Castle Wedding
articles.summary: Rene Barnes created six looks using deadstock fabric from Dior, Armani, and Oscar de la Renta to marry Christian DiCroce at a 13th-century castle outside Siena.
body: The pair decided to tie the knot exactly one year later on May 8, 2026, at Castello di Celsa in Italy. Says the bride, “The first time we drove through the gates, I just looked at him, and we both knew this was where we wanted to get married.” Adds the groom, “It just felt like us.” The couple brought an intimate group of friends and family to witness them exchange vows. “We wanted the weekend to feel like an experience rather than just a wedding, so we planned a few days for everyone to slow down and celebrate together,” says Rene.

Naturally, the designer also created all her jewelry for the weekend. “Every piece was designed and made specifically for the look it accompanied, using old European diamonds throughout the collection,” she shares. “I also created our matching wedding bands and a custom diamond brooch for Christian.”

articles.title: This App Will Make You Want to Use the Pixel 11 Pro's 'HiLight' Feature
articles.summary: We may earn a commission from links on this page. When Google announced the Pixel 11 series last week, it showed off a new "upgrade" for its Pro devices—including the Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL, and Pixel 11 Pro Fold.
body: Unfortunately, there's nothing else HiLight can do out of the box, which seems like a big missed opportunity for a brand-new hardware feature. Google wants customers to spend more for a Pro device, only to give them two things to do with this Pixel 11 Pro exclusive. And while there's certainly some utility in assigning contacts different colors, to silently know who's calling without needing to pick up your Pixel, there are so many other possibilities for HiLight that the current iteration feels way underbaked.

Enter: HiLight Studio, a new app from developer DhananjayBhosale. DhanajayBhosale's announcement appeared on my X feed, and it immediately caught my attention. The developer designed the app to take full advantage of Google's new hardware, even if Google isn't taking advantage itself. With HiLight Studio, you can assign colors and effects for notifications from any app on your Pixel, not just contacts. Chrome alerts can be blue, WhatsApp alerts can be green, and so on. In addition, you can effectively choose any shade of any color that Android allows, down to saturation and intensity levels.

articles.title: What Garmin's 'Recovery Time' Estimate Actually Means
articles.summary: We may earn a commission from links on this page. Garmin's fitness watches often give you a "recovery time" after a workout. For example, after one easy run, it told me that I need 21 hours before I'll fully recover.
body: You’ll see your recovery time in the end-of-workout summary that you get right after you finish a workout on many Garmin watches. It’s also available from the Training Status glance on your watch, or the Training Readiness tile in the Garmin Connect app if you have that. On my Forerunner 570, I can even set it as one of the little complications on my main watch face. The recovery time feature is available on most Enduro, Epix, Fenix, Forerunner, Instinct, Venu, and Vivoactive watches, among others (Garmin has a full list here ).

Garmin defines recovery time as “an estimate on how long it will take for you to fully recover and be ready for your next workout of the same intensity.” Note that phrase, fully recover. No athlete is fully recovered at the start of every training session; it's normal to carry a little fatigue from one session to the next. This number is just giving you a sense of how long you’ll be feeling the effects of this workout.
points: Garmin's fitness watches often give you a "recovery time" after a workout.
